clinicalScope: Red blood cell structure, function and the most common adult disorders (anemia, polycythemia, hemolysis) encountered on ward rounds in East African and other low‑resource hospitals
title: Red Blood Cell: Physiology and Common Disorders
subject: Medicine
summary: Red blood cells (RBCs) are the tiny, biconcave cells that carry oxygen from the lungs to tissues and return carbon dioxide. In low‑resource settings, clinicians most often see disorders that change the number or quality of RBCs, such as anemia, polycythemia and hemolysis.

sections.p: Red blood cells are anucleate, biconcave cells whose main role is gas transport. In sub‑Saharan Africa, anemia affects up to 60 % of women of reproductive age and 30 % of children, while polycythemia is rare but may follow chronic hypoxia (e.g., high altitude, COPD).
b: Normal adult RBC count: 4.5–5.9 million/µL (men), 4.0–5.2 million/µL (women)
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 80–100 fL indicates normocytic size
Hemoglobin (Hb) normal: ≥13 g/dL (men), ≥12 g/dL (women)
Prevalence of sickle‑cell disease in East Africa ≈1‑2 % of newborns

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, the leading causes of abnormal RBC indices are nutritional deficiencies, infectious diseases and inherited hemoglobinopathies.
b: Iron deficiency from malaria, hookworm, menstrual loss – most common anemia
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency – malnutrition, chronic alcoholism
Sickle‑cell disease and trait – hereditary, high prevalence in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda
Chronic kidney disease – reduced erythropoietin production
Chronic hypoxia (COPD, high altitude) – secondary polycythemia

sections.p: Erythropoiesis occurs in red marrow under erythropoietin (EPO) control; deficiencies or destruction alter RBC mass.
b: Iron deficiency limits hemoglobin synthesis → microcytic, hypochromic cells
Vitamin B12/folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis → macrocytic, megaloblastic cells
Sickle‑cell polymerisation under low O₂ → rigid cells, vaso‑occlusion, hemolysis
Autoimmune hemolysis: antibodies bind RBCs → splenic clearance
EPO excess (e.g., high altitude) → increased RBC production → polycythemia

sections.p: Patients present with symptoms reflecting oxygen delivery, blood viscosity or hemolysis.
b: Fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, pallor – anemia
Jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly – hemolysis
Headache, dizziness, ruddy complexion, hypertension – polycythemia
Chest pain or vaso‑occlusive crisis in sickle‑cell disease
Rapid heart rate (tachycardia) as compensatory response

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical can narrow the differential before labs.
b: Ask about diet, menstrual history, deworming, malaria episodes, sickle‑cell family history
Enquire about recent infections, drug exposures (e.g., dapsone), altitude travel
Inspect for pallor of conjunctivae, nail beds, and tongue; note jaundice
Palpate spleen (enlargement suggests hemolysis or infection)
Measure blood pressure and pulse; high BP may accompany polycythemia

sections.p: Distinguish anemia types, hemolysis, and polycythemia based on history, exam and simple labs.
b: Microcytic anemia: iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease
Normocytic anemia: acute blood loss, hemolysis, chronic kidney disease
Macrocytic anemia: B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism
Secondary polycythemia: chronic hypoxia, COPD, high altitude
Primary polycythemia (PV) – rare, JAK2 mutation, not typical in low‑resource settings

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Basic haematology plus targeted tests guide diagnosis; alternatives are offered when equipment is lacking.

t.b: Quantifies RBC count, Hb, Hct, MCV, MCHC – determines anemia vs polycythemia and cell size
Looks for shape abnormalities (sickle cells, schistocytes) – confirms hemolysis or specific disorders
Low ferritin confirms iron‑deficiency anemia; if unavailable, use transferrin saturation
Elevated (>2 %) indicates marrow response (hemolysis or blood loss); low suggests production problem
Low levels diagnose macrocytic anemia; if unavailable, use methylmalonic acid (if possible) or clinical clues
Low in intravascular hemolysis; if not available, rely on LDH, bilirubin and smear

sections.p: Severity guides urgency of treatment and need for transfusion.
b: Mild anemia: Hb 10‑12 g/dL – observe, oral iron if iron‑deficient
Moderate anemia: Hb 7‑9 g/dL – consider transfusion if symptomatic or pregnant
Severe anemia: Hb < 7 g/dL – urgent packed RBC transfusion
Polycythemia: Hct > 55 % – risk of thrombosis, consider phlebotomy if symptomatic
Hemolytic crisis: rapid Hb drop > 2 g/dL in 24 h – admit, start supportive care

sections.p: Co‑existing conditions may mask or worsen RBC disorders.
b: Malaria can cause both anemia (hemolysis) and splenomegaly
HIV infection predisposes to anemia of chronic disease and opportunistic marrow suppression
Chronic kidney disease reduces EPO – anemia may persist despite iron repletion
Pregnancy dilutes blood volume, lowering Hb without true loss of RBCs
Altitude exposure temporarily raises Hb, potentially confusing polycythemia assessment

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, replace deficits, and monitor for complications.
b: Sickle‑cell crisis: analgesia, hydration, oxygen, consider blood transfusion if severe
Hemolysis from malaria: parenteral artesunate followed by ACT; monitor Hb
Severe anemia (Hb < 7 g/dL): transfuse packed RBCs, target Hb ≥ 9 g/dL in pregnancy
EPO therapy for chronic kidney disease when Hb < 10 g/dL and iron stores adequate
High‑output cardiac failure from chronic severe anemia – dyspnea, peripheral edema
Acute chest syndrome in sickle‑cell disease – chest pain, hypoxia, new infiltrate
Thromboembolism in polycythemia – sudden dyspnea, leg swelling
Hyperbilirubinemia causing kernicterus in newborns – yellow sclera, lethargy
Sepsis in patients with severe anemia or splenomegaly – fever, hypotension

sections.p: Pregnant women, children and patients with HIV need tailored approaches.
b: Pregnancy: lower Hb thresholds for treatment; iron tablets safe, avoid high‑dose folate excess
Children <5 y: use weight‑based iron dosing; monitor growth and developmental milestones
HIV‑positive: screen for zidovudine‑induced anemia, treat opportunistic infections
Sickle‑cell disease: prophylactic penicillin in children, vaccination against encapsulated organisms
Elderly: consider comorbid cardiac disease before transfusion

sections.p: Most anemia causes are reversible with proper therapy; prevention focuses on nutrition and infection control.
b: Iron‑deficiency: repeat Hb in 4 weeks; expect rise of 1‑2 g/dL per month
Sickle‑cell disease: life expectancy now > 50 y with comprehensive care
Polycythemia: regular phlebotomy reduces thrombotic risk; monitor Hct every 3‑6 months
Prevent malaria‑related anemia with insecticide‑treated nets and intermittent preventive therapy
Deworming programs and iron‑fortified foods lower community anemia rates

sections.p: Certain lab patterns may be falsely normal or abnormal in low‑resource settings.
b: Ferritin is an acute‑phase reactant; it may be normal or high during infection despite iron deficiency
Reticulocyte count can be falsely low if sample is delayed or stored improperly
Peripheral smear quality may suffer without a good microscope, missing subtle schistocytes
Hematocrit may be overestimated in dehydration; correct with clinical assessment of volume status

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in hemoglobin >2 g/dL within 24 h
Chest pain, dyspnea, or new hypoxia in a sickle‑cell patient
Signs of high‑output heart failure (rapid breathing, peripheral edema) in severe anemia
Neurological changes with jaundice suggesting bilirubin encephalopathy

faq.q: Why does iron deficiency cause microcytic anemia?
faq.a: Lack of iron limits hemoglobin synthesis, so red cells are produced smaller to conserve resources.

faq.q: Can a patient have both anemia and polycythemia?
faq.a: Yes, in mixed disorders such as sickle‑cell disease with chronic hemolysis (anemia) and secondary polycythemia from hypoxia.

faq.q: What is the first test if a malaria‑endemic patient presents with severe anemia?
faq.a: A rapid diagnostic test (RDT) for malaria, followed by a full blood count to assess hemoglobin.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman from rural Kenya presents with fatigue, pallor and a diet low in meat; Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 72 fL. What is the most likely diagnosis and first‑line treatment? — Iron‑deficiency anemia; start oral ferrous sulfate with vitamin C, counsel on dietary iron.

A 5‑year‑old boy with sickle‑cell disease develops chest pain, fever, and a new infiltrate on chest X‑ray. Which complication should you suspect and what immediate step is required? — Acute chest syndrome; give supplemental oxygen, analgesia, and consider blood transfusion.

A patient with chronic kidney disease has Hb 9 g/dL despite iron supplementation. Which medication is indicated and why? — Erythropoiesis‑stimulating agent (EPO) because renal production of EPO is insufficient.

During a malaria outbreak, a 12‑year‑old has Hb 6 g/dL and a positive malaria RDT. What are the transfusion thresholds and why? — Transfuse packed RBCs if Hb < 7 g/dL or symptomatic; aim to raise Hb above 7‑8 g/dL to improve oxygen delivery.

A 45‑year‑old smoker living at 2500 m altitude has Hb 18 g/dL, Hct 55 %. What is the most likely cause and first management? — Secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxia; low‑dose aspirin and consider phlebotomy if symptomatic.

A patient presents with jaundice, dark urine, and a reticulocyte count of 5 %. Which laboratory test will confirm intravascular hemolysis and what result is expected? — Low haptoglobin; a result < 0.1 g/L supports intravascular hemolysis.
In a resource‑limited clinic, the hemoglobinometer is unavailable. Which bedside sign can help estimate severe anemia? — Marked conjunctival pallor combined with tachycardia and exertional dyspnea.
Why might ferritin be normal in a patient with iron‑deficiency anemia who also has malaria? — Ferritin rises as an acute‑phase reactant during infection, masking iron deficiency.

A 60‑year‑old with COPD has Hb 17 g/dL, Hct 52 %. He complains of headache and visual disturbances. What complication is he at risk for and how can you reduce it? — Thromboembolic events; give low‑dose aspirin and maintain hydration.

During a blood transfusion, the patient develops fever and chills after 15 minutes. What is the most likely cause and immediate action? — Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction; stop transfusion, maintain IV access, and start supportive care.
